# Methodology {#sec-methodology}

This chapter specifies how the model--harness systems introduced in @sec-introduction are compared. Harness-native behavior is preserved where it is part of the system under study, while external differences such as routing, context limits, model selection, and usage accounting are controlled when necessary for comparability. Configuration details that are needed only to reproduce or audit the runs are collected in @sec-appendix-setup.

## Benchmark and task selection

DeepSWE v1.1 was selected during planning in July--August 2026. Its isolated functional verifiers provide a binary pass/fail criterion without an LLM judge [@huang2026deepswe], avoiding the need to construct and validate a new internal task set.

Running the complete benchmark across all model--harness combinations was outside the available budget. A deterministic subset of ten tasks was therefore selected from the public DeepSWE v1.1 results: one hard and one medium task for each programming language, with difficulty derived from the solve rate of historical `mini-swe-agent` runs. Within each language and difficulty group, the task with the highest median historical token usage is selected. This deliberately favors demanding tasks on which differences in context handling and token efficiency are more likely to become visible. @tbl-tasks lists the tasks under the short names used in the following chapters; the complete selection procedure is documented in @sec-appendix-task-selection.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-tasks
#| tbl-cap: "The ten benchmark tasks. The solve rate is that of the historical `mini-swe-agent` runs from which the difficulty was derived."
#| tbl-colwidths: [22, 14, 12, 34, 18]

import json as _json
from pathlib import Path as _Path

from IPython.display import Markdown as _Markdown

_LANGUAGES = {"go": "Go", "javascript": "JavaScript", "python": "Python", "rust": "Rust", "typescript": "TypeScript"}
_selection = _json.loads(_Path("data/deepswe_task_selection_v1.1.json").read_text())["selected_tasks"]
_tasks = ["| Task | Language | Difficulty | Repository | Solve rate |", "|:--|:--|:--|:--|--:|"]
for _task in sorted(_selection, key=lambda t: (t["language"], t["stratum"] != "hard")):
    _short = "python-statemachine" if _task["task_id"].startswith("python-") else _task["task_id"].split("-")[0]
    _tasks.append(f"| `{_short}` | {_LANGUAGES[_task['language']]} | {_task['stratum']} "
                  f"| `{_task['repository']}` | {100 * _task['solve_rate']:.0f}% |")
_Markdown("\n".join(_tasks))
```

## Model and harness selection

The four harnesses were selected for complementary practical reasons. Claude Code and Codex represent first-party coding agents from major model providers. OpenCode was the second-most common first-choice harness in the internal survey described in @sec-current-state, while Pi provides a comparatively lightweight alternative. OpenCode V2 was selected instead of V1 because it is the current major redesign and is more representative of the tool's future development. The models were selected to span several providers and price classes and are run at `max` reasoning effort where the retained configuration permits.

The planned model--harness cross-product could not be completed within the fixed evaluation budget. The first Fireworks-backed GLM-5.3-Flash run consumed most of the remaining pay-as-you-go budget [@pa1GlmRouteData; @pa1Issue71Budget], so Kimi K3 was not run with OpenCode V2. GPT-5.6 Luna was retained across all four harnesses by routing it through the researcher's personal ChatGPT subscription instead of incurring further pay-as-you-go API expenditure [@pa1Issue71Budget]. Several runs were later excluded or repeated because of gateway defects that only became visible in the analysis; @sec-measurement-corrections describes these defects, and @sec-benchmark-coverage shows the resulting benchmark matrix.

## Experimental controls

Each trial evaluates exactly one model through one harness. Harness-native delegation remains enabled because subagent orchestration is part of the behavior under study. However, delegated calls are constrained to the same benchmark model as the parent session. This prevents a nominally single-model trial from becoming a multi-model ensemble. Usage is aggregated across the complete parent/child session tree.

Provider-specific harness optimizations are otherwise retained. For example, a harness may use its native compaction or caching behavior when the selected model supports it. Equivalent features are not recreated through custom plugins in competing harnesses, because the objective is to evaluate the harnesses as practical systems rather than force their internal implementations to be identical.

GPT-5.6 Luna supports a larger API context window, but the first-party Codex 0.151.0 model profile uses 272,000 tokens as its default context window and requires an explicit override to use more [@codex0151ModelCatalog]. OpenAI also applies higher pricing when a request exceeds 272,000 input tokens [@openaiGpt56Luna]. The experiment therefore adopts the same 272,000-token operating window recommended by the first-party Codex default for every harness. Allowing only some harnesses to use the larger window would make cost depend on inconsistent context configuration and could move one harness into a different pricing tier.

External web-search capability is disabled in the benchmark configuration wherever the harness exposes a controllable search tool. This keeps trials limited to the repository, benchmark environment, and harness-native development tools rather than allowing external information retrieval.

### Model profiles

Where a harness ships a provider or model profile for a tested model, that profile is used as the base configuration. Only settings required to reach the designated inference endpoint are changed, such as the base URL, credentials, or gateway-facing model identifier. A custom profile is introduced only when the pinned harness version has no usable entry for the tested model or when the selected provider route requires narrowly scoped transport metadata (@sec-appendix-profiles).

One exception changes the evaluated system. Codex 0.151.0 ships a native profile for GPT-5.6 Luna, but not for Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, or GLM-5.3-Flash. Unknown models receive a minimal fallback descriptor without configured multi-agent mode or tool mode, model-specific reasoning levels, and several other profile features available to recognized models [@codex0151FallbackMetadata]. For these three models, the experiment therefore derives the Codex metadata from the frozen GPT-5.6 Sol profile and replaces only the model-specific identity, context, modality, reasoning, and compatibility fields. Codex results for these models are conditional on this Sol-derived profile.

### Model routing

@tbl-routes summarizes how each model was reached. Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and GLM-5.3-Flash are routed through AiOrbit, the internal LiteLLM gateway used by the organization, and are served through Fireworks behind it. GPT-5.6 Luna is accessed through the researcher's personal ChatGPT subscription via a pinned CLIProxyAPI instance, which exposes the same subscription-backed route to all four harnesses [@cliproxyCodexOAuth]. CLIProxyAPI also serves as a protocol bridge where a harness cannot talk to the gateway directly. Its own retries, credential cooldowns, and model fallbacks are disabled, so it translates requests without changing the measured harness behavior. @sec-appendix-routing documents the bridge configuration.

| Model | Route | Harnesses |
|:------|:------|:----------|
| Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash | AiOrbit (LiteLLM) → Fireworks | Pi, OpenCode V2 |
| | CLIProxyAPI (Responses → Chat Completions) → AiOrbit → Fireworks | Codex |
| | AiOrbit's Anthropic translation → Fireworks (original runs); CLIProxyAPI with `is-compat: true` → AiOrbit → Fireworks (repeated runs) | Claude Code |
| GPT-5.6 Luna | CLIProxyAPI → ChatGPT subscription | all four |

: Provider routes per model and harness. The two Claude Code routes are compared in @sec-claude-code-reasoning. {#tbl-routes tbl-colwidths="[26,52,22]"}

AiOrbit, Fireworks, and CLIProxyAPI are infrastructure outside the experimental manipulation. They may transform requests or introduce provider-side failures that the study cannot control. The results therefore characterize the harnesses under these documented deployment paths rather than an abstract provider-independent environment.

## Benchmark infrastructure

Trials are executed by a project-specific fork of the Pier runner [@pierUpstream; @pierFzrFork]. The fork adds Pi and OpenCode V2 adapters, enforces the same-model control for delegated calls, and counts token and cache usage across all subagent sessions. These changes affect agent installation, routing, model enforcement, trajectory conversion, and measurement, but do not modify the DeepSWE task description, repository, verifier, or reward calculation presented to the agent. @sec-appendix-pier lists the changes, and @sec-appendix-opencode describes the OpenCode V2 integration.

The harness versions are fixed at Codex CLI 0.151.0, Claude Code 2.1.251, Pi 0.84.4, and OpenCode V2 2.0.8, and DeepSWE at a fixed revision. The Pier fork moved through four checkpoints during the benchmark; @sec-appendix-checkpoints records which runs used which checkpoint and why the differences do not affect the retained measurements.

## Retries and canonical attempts {#sec-canonical-attempts}

Every benchmark configuration allows Pier to repeat a complete trial once. The retry was intended to replace attempts invalidated by transport or gateway failures; agent timeouts, verifier timeouts, missing or invalid reward outputs, and operator cancellations remain final. In practice, Pier also repeated some trials that had failed because of the evaluated model or harness (@sec-retry-eligibility).

Each model--harness--task combination therefore enters the analysis with exactly one canonical attempt. If a transport or gateway failure invalidated the first attempt, Pier's final attempt is canonical. If the first attempt ended because of the evaluated model or harness, for example when OpenCode V2 aborted the session because the model had asked a question, the first attempt is canonical, whether it failed or passed. The retry was then a second chance that the evaluated system should not have received. All success, token, cache, and cost results are computed from the same canonical attempt.

## Cost accounting {#sec-cost-accounting}

Cross-harness cost is calculated from recorded token and cache usage using a frozen pricing table. Official model API prices are used rather than the invoice price of the underlying proxy, inference host, or subscription. GPT-5.6 Luna is executed through a flat-rate ChatGPT subscription, so its reported dollar cost is an API-equivalent normalization derived from recorded token usage rather than the marginal amount charged for the benchmark run. This separates model and harness efficiency from provider-specific billing arrangements.

Comparative cost includes only the tokens of the canonical attempt. Non-canonical attempts still consumed budget, but they are not attributed to a model--harness observation: an attempt invalidated by a transport failure reflects the infrastructure, and a retry after a model or harness failure is an unintended second chance. Their cost is reported separately as experimental overhead.

## Metrics and analysis {#sec-metrics}

A trial passes when the task's verifier accepts the final repository state. The verifier runs fail-to-pass tests, new tests that the change must satisfy, and previously passing (pass-to-pass) tests of the repository, which guard against regressions [@huang2026deepswe]. A change that implements the requested functionality but breaks existing behavior therefore fails the task. The number of fail-to-pass tests that pass shows how close a failing trial came to a solution.

Cost is the API-equivalent cost computed from the recorded token usage (@sec-cost-accounting). The cost per passing trial divides the total cost of a condition's ten trials by its number of passing trials. Because totals can be dominated by single expensive tasks, harnesses are also compared task by task, as the geometric mean of their per-task ratios to a reference harness; the same measure is applied to tokens, agent steps, and agent time. The cache-hit share is the fraction of a trial's input tokens that was read from the prompt cache. A harness lies on the Pareto front of a model when no other harness passed at least as many tasks at a lower cost, or, in the second view, with fewer input and output tokens.

An invocation error is a tool call rejected because of the call itself. This covers invalid arguments or script syntax, edits whose old text was not found or not unique, missing files, and out-of-range offsets. Non-zero shell exits are not counted, because a failing test or an empty search is often the intended result. Context use is described by the largest prompt of a trial and by the number of compactions.

Every condition uses the same ten tasks, so comparisons within a model are paired by task. Whether a difference in success between two harnesses could be chance is checked with an exact two-sided sign test. The test considers only the tasks that exactly one of the two harnesses solved and gives the probability p of a split at least this uneven if each of these tasks were equally likely to go to either harness. With ten tasks per condition, p stays above the conventional threshold of 5% in every harness comparison, so differences in success are reported descriptively rather than as established effects. The data files and analysis scripts behind every result are listed in @sec-appendix-data.
